nodes.title: BGP: Key Ideas
nodes.content: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the routing protocol of the internet. It runs between autonomous systems (ASes) and is a path-vector protocol — instead of a metric, each route carries the full list of ASes it has traversed.

flashcards.back: eBGP runs between routers in different ASes; it's how the internet is glued together. iBGP runs between routers inside the same AS — it carries external routes to internal routers. iBGP requires a full mesh (or route reflectors) because routes learned via iBGP are NOT re-advertised to other iBGP peers.

flashcards.front: What is AS_PATH and why does it matter?
flashcards.back: AS_PATH is the list of autonomous systems a route has traversed, prepended at each AS boundary. It's the primary loop-prevention mechanism (a router rejects a route already containing its own AS) and the second tie-breaker in BGP best-path selection — shorter path wins.

flashcards.front: BGP best-path attributes — name the top three.
flashcards.back: (1) Highest LOCAL_PREF wins (locally configured 'prefer this exit'). (2) Shortest AS_PATH. (3) Lowest ORIGIN code (IGP < EGP < incomplete). Then MED, then eBGP > iBGP, then lowest IGP cost, then router-ID tie-breaker. LOCAL_PREF is how you steer outbound; AS_PATH prepending is how you influence inbound.

flashcards.front: Why does BGP need a route reflector?
flashcards.back: iBGP requires a full mesh (every router peers with every other) — O(n²) sessions, doesn't scale. A route reflector breaks the rule: it re-advertises iBGP routes to its clients. Clients only peer with the RR. One RR + 100 clients = 100 sessions vs. 5,000 for a full mesh.

pairs.stem: What is VXLAN and what problem does it solve?
pairs.option: Virtual eXtensible LAN — encapsulates Layer 2 frames in UDP (port 4789), extending Layer 2 domains across Layer 3 infrastructure. Supports 16 million VNIs vs VLAN's 4094 limit.

pairs.stem: What is LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol) and why is it used in SD-Access?
pairs.option: LISP separates device identity (EID) from location (RLOC), enabling endpoint mobility and scalable routing in Cisco SD-Access fabric. The control plane uses LISP to map EIDs to RLOCs.

nodes.title: IP routing: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Routing is how packets find their way through a multi-network internet. Every router runs a forwarding table; routing protocols (OSPF, EIGRP, BGP) are the mechanisms by which routers exchange information and build that table.

flashcards.back: When multiple routes match a destination, the router picks the one with the most-specific (longest) prefix. So `10.0.0.0/24` beats `10.0.0.0/16` for a packet to `10.0.0.5`. This is how more-specific routes can override defaults.

It matches every destination, so it's used only when no more-specific route exists. Typically points to the internet gateway. On a stub network, the default route is often the ONLY route — everything not local goes 'up' to a smarter router.

flashcards.front: Static vs dynamic routing — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Static routes are hand-configured, easy to understand, perfect for small or stub networks. Dynamic routing (OSPF, BGP, EIGRP) auto-discovers topology, reacts to link failures, scales to thousands of routers. Use dynamic the moment the topology is non-trivial or expected to change.

When the same destination is learned from multiple sources (static + OSPF + BGP), the router prefers the one with the lowest administrative distance. Defaults (Cisco): connected=0, static=1, EIGRP=90, OSPF=110, BGP=200. It's the tie-breaker before the routing-protocol metric.

pairs.stem: What is Cisco ACI (Application Centric Infrastructure)?
pairs.option: A data center SDN solution using intent-based networking — physical/virtual infrastructure managed via APIC controller using policy objects: Tenants, EPGs, Contracts, and Bridge Domains.

pairs.stem: What is a route leak in BGP and how is it prevented?
What is the difference between VXLAN with flood-and-learn vs EVPN control plane?
What is EIGRP Feasible Condition and Feasible Successor?
pairs.option: A backup route that is guaranteed loop-free because its Advertised Distance (AD) is less than the current successor's Feasible Distance (FD). Immediately usable without recomputation upon successor failure.

pairs.stem: What is an OSPF virtual link?
pairs.option: Connects a non-backbone OSPF area that lacks a direct physical connection to Area 0 — the virtual link traverses a transit area and logically extends the Area 0 backbone.

nodes.title: OSPF: Key Ideas
nodes.content: OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) is a link-state interior gateway protocol — every router floods its neighbors with link-state advertisements (LSAs), builds an identical map of the network, and runs Dijkstra to find shortest paths.

flashcards.front: What is an OSPF area, and why use multiple?
flashcards.back: An area is a group of OSPF routers that share full link-state info. ABRs (area border routers) summarize between areas. Single-area is fine for small networks (~50 routers); multi-area limits LSA flooding scope and reduces SPF computation as the network grows.
The backbone area. All non-zero areas MUST connect to area 0, directly or via a virtual link. Inter-area traffic always passes through area 0. If area 0 partitions, OSPF breaks.

Default cost = reference-bandwidth ÷ interface-bandwidth. Reference defaults to 100 Mbps, so a 100 Mbps link costs 1, a 10 Mbps link costs 10. On modern networks you should raise the reference (e.g., to 1000) so 1G+ links get distinguishable costs.

flashcards.front: DR / BDR — what problem do they solve?
flashcards.back: On a multi-access segment (Ethernet), if every router formed a full adjacency with every other, you'd get O(n²) flooding. OSPF elects a Designated Router (DR) and Backup DR. Other routers only fully adjacency with the DR/BDR; the DR re-floods. The election uses priority then router ID.

pairs.stem: What is Cisco APIC-EM vs Cisco DNA Center?
pairs.option: APIC-EM was the older SDN controller (deprecated 2019). DNA Center replaced it with enhanced IBN capabilities: intent-based networking, AI analytics, SD-Access, and full lifecycle management.

pairs.stem: What is NHRP in DMVPN?
What is OSPF external route redistribution Type 1 vs Type 2?
What is Cisco IOS-XE vs IOS-XR vs NX-OS?
pairs.option: IOS-XE: modular version of IOS for ASR/ISR/Cat — runs on Linux kernel, supports IOS programmability. IOS-XR: carrier-grade for ASR9K/NCS, high availability, in-service software upgrade. NX-OS: data center OS for Nexus switches.

pairs.stem: What is LACP rate and what does 'fast' mode do?
pairs.option: Changes LACP PDU interval from slow (30s) to fast (1s) — detects link failures or partner changes within 3 seconds instead of 90 seconds, improving failover speed.

nodes.title: Security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.
Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.
Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.

pairs.stem: What is the purpose of OSPF Hello packets?
pairs.option: Discover and maintain neighbor relationships. Hellos contain: router ID, area ID, Hello/Dead intervals, DR/BDR addresses, auth, and neighbor list. Parameters must match on both sides for adjacency.

pairs.stem: What is Cisco Umbrella?
pairs.option: A cloud-delivered DNS security service that blocks malicious domains/IPs at the DNS layer — before connections are established, protecting on and off-network users.
